claims.text: Loss of toughness in initially single-phase high-entropy alloys at intermediate temperatures is governed by rapid nanosegregation of principal elements to grain boundaries.
Cr, Mn, and Ni are principal elements that segregate to grain boundaries in the proposed CrMnFeCoNi alloy.
Grain-boundary nanosegregation locally reduces cohesion and triggers intergranular brittle fracture.
Embrittlement in conventional alloys is induced by brittle grain-boundary precipitation rather than the proposed segregation mechanism.
Exposure or deformation at 500–700°C under service-relevant strain rates promotes nanoscale Cr-, Mn-, and Ni-enriched clusters along grain boundaries.
At intermediate temperatures and without long aging, thermal activation enables rapid short-range diffusion of principal elements to grain boundaries.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion localizes stress and initiates brittle intergranular cracks under mechanical loading.
Intermediate-temperature samples exhibiting grain-boundary nanosegregation will show reduced ductility and a transition toward intergranular fracture.
Preexisting Cr-rich precipitates can act as sinks for mobile embrittling elements.
High-entropy alloys containing such Cr-rich precipitates should exhibit improved ductility and more uniform fracture behavior.
The same single-phase alloy tested at room temperature exhibits high toughness and ductile transgranular fracture without significant grain-boundary embrittlement.
The proposed segregation-driven embrittlement is most pronounced at 500–700°C and moderate strain rates.
At very high temperatures, other diffusion or phase-separation phenomena dominate over the proposed mechanism.
At very low temperatures, suppressed segregation kinetics render the proposed mechanism inactive or less active.
Minor impurity levels and variations in alloy composition affect segregation behavior and the embrittlement threshold.

contradictions.description: The proposed comparison calls both sets microstructurally similar single-phase samples, but the pre-treated set is deliberately given Cr-rich secondary precipitates at grain boundaries and therefore is neither single-phase nor fully microstructurally matched.
